headline:
Who will be there
between visits?
support: A practical question for Westlake Village families

GBP.title: Westlake Village: planning support between hospice visits
GBP.caption:
Hospice at home in Westlake Village begins with a practical question: who will be there between visits?

Hospice care follows an individualized plan. Hospice services include scheduled visits and clinical support available by phone 24/7—not continuous bedside nursing or a live-in caregiver.

At Eternal Life Hospice, a hospice consultation starts with the person’s wishes and the household’s practical needs. Our Journal guide offers questions about daily help, family schedules, care-team contacts and what to do when needs change.

Read the guide to prepare for your family’s care conversation.

Facebook.title: A care plan also needs a plan between visits
Facebook.caption:
Hospice at home needs a plan for the hours between visits.

For Westlake Village families, it helps to talk through the ordinary parts of the day: who can be present, who can help with daily needs and whom to call when something changes.

Hospice care follows an individualized plan. Clinical guidance available by phone 24/7 does not mean a nurse stays at the bedside around the clock or that hospice provides a live-in caregiver.

At Eternal Life Hospice, a hospice consultation begins with listening. You do not have to have every answer before you ask about hospice services or the support your household may need.

#WestlakeVillage #FamilyCaregiving #HospiceCare

LinkedIn.title: Make the hours between hospice visits part of the conversation
LinkedIn.caption:
Planning hospice at home means planning for the hours between visits.

For families and referral partners, understanding hospice services is only part of preparing for care at home. Daily support, household availability and an agreed contact for changes in needs deserve equal clarity.

An individualized hospice care plan does not establish continuous bedside staffing. Clinical support available by phone 24/7 is distinct from live-in caregiving or around-the-clock nursing in the home.

At Eternal Life Hospice, a hospice consultation starts with the person’s wishes and the household’s practical needs. Clear expectations can help families identify what still needs to be arranged.

Our Westlake Village Journal guide provides a starting point for that discussion.

headline:
Before you sign,
ask your questions.

GBP.title: The hospice election statement: a conversation, not a test
GBP.caption:
Does Medicare cover hospice at home? What does the election statement mean for hospice care cost?

These are questions worth discussing before signing. The hospice election statement records important choices about hospice care and coverage. Ask which hospice services relate to the terminal illness and which costs or services may fall outside the benefit.

Eternal Life Hospice’s Journal guide offers a plain-language starting point. An election statement, an advance directive and decision-maker documents serve different purposes; your care team can help clarify the distinctions.

Read the guide and bring your questions to the team.

headline:
Comfort starts
with permission.
support: Listening first. Respecting each person’s choice.

GBP.title: Personalized comfort begins with a choice
GBP.caption:
Comfort care begins with asking—not assuming.

For someone receiving hospice care, a familiar routine, gentle sound or simply quiet may feel welcome. The person’s wishes guide the choice.

At Eternal Life Hospice, optional sound bathing may offer a setting for relaxation and feeling more settled. It is not a medical treatment and does not replace symptom assessment, medications or licensed care. Choosing silence deserves the same respect.

Our Journal article explores consent, optional nonclinical support and how personal preferences guide the conversation.

Read “Personalized Comfort Starts With Permission.”

Facebook.title: Comfort starts with permission
Facebook.caption:
Sometimes the most thoughtful question is, “Would you like this—or would you prefer quiet?”

Comfort care is personal. A familiar routine, gentle sound or a calm moment can mean different things to different people, and a person’s choice can change from day to day.

At Eternal Life Hospice, optional sound bathing is offered as a preference-led comfort experience—a space for relaxation and feeling more grounded, not a medical treatment. Some people may welcome it. Others may choose silence. Both choices deserve respect.

This optional experience does not replace symptom assessment, medications or licensed hospice care. Sound bathing is not covered by Medicare or Medi-Cal; Eternal provides it at no additional expense to families, subject to availability and fit.

Read how permission shapes personalized comfort: {url}

#PersonCenteredCare #HospiceComfort #EternalLifeHospice

LinkedIn.title: Person-centered comfort begins with permission
LinkedIn.caption:
Comfort care is only person-centered when declining an optional offering is a genuine choice.

For people receiving hospice care, personalization begins with listening to wishes, routines and privacy preferences—not with assuming that the same experience will feel comforting to everyone.

At Eternal Life Hospice, optional sound bathing is framed as a preference-led opportunity for relaxation and feeling more settled. It is not offered to diagnose, treat or cure, and it does not replace symptom assessment, medications or licensed care.

A person may welcome gentle sound, prefer a familiar routine or choose quiet. Consent can change, and the plan should respect that.

Sound bathing is not covered by Medicare or Medi-Cal. Eternal provides it at no additional expense to families, subject to availability and fit.

Our Journal article explores these boundaries and the role of optional nonclinical support.

#PersonCenteredCare #HospiceCare #PatientChoice

headline:
A thoughtful
care handoff.
support: Planning a thoughtful care handoff in Calabasas

GBP.title: Calabasas: planning a thoughtful care handoff
GBP.caption:
Planning hospice care in Calabasas during a move to assisted living involves more than transferring a medication list.

Whether you are exploring hospice at home or discussing care in a residence, share familiar routines, communication preferences, privacy boundaries and the names of the people who should receive updates.

Clarify responsibilities between the residence and hospice team, including daily assistance, medication coordination and after-hours contacts. Hospice services do not replace the facility’s staffing or provide continuous bedside nursing.

Eternal Life Hospice’s Journal checklist offers questions to help families plan a thoughtful handoff. Read the guide.

headline:
Keep what
feels familiar.
support: Small traditions. Room for rest. A person’s choice.

GBP.title: Keeping familiar traditions during hospice care
GBP.caption:
A tradition can become smaller and still feel meaningful.

A familiar photograph, favorite music or a short visit may be enough to keep a sense of connection. During hospice care, the person’s energy, comfort and wishes can guide what the day looks like—including choosing rest or quiet instead.

At Eternal Life Hospice, comfort care begins with listening. Our Journal article explores ways families can keep ordinary seasonal traditions flexible, without making participation an expectation.

Read “Keeping Ordinary Traditions During Hospice Care.”

Facebook.title: A smaller tradition can still feel like yours
Facebook.caption:
A smaller tradition can still feel like yours.

A favorite photograph. Familiar music. A short visit with someone who understands when it is time to rest.

During hospice care, a meaningful day does not have to look the way it used to. Traditions can change with a person’s energy and wishes, without becoming another thing the family feels it must get right.

At Eternal Life Hospice, comfort care begins with listening to what feels welcome today. Make room for a different answer tomorrow. Choosing quiet or sitting something out is a choice worth honoring, too.

Our Journal article shares a thoughtful approach to keeping ordinary traditions familiar and manageable.

Read the article: {url}

#FamilyConnection #HospiceCare #CareThatHonorsLife

LinkedIn.title: Familiar routines belong in person-centered care
LinkedIn.caption:
Familiar routines belong in hospice care—with room for the person to change their mind.

Seasonal traditions can carry meaning for a person receiving care. A familiar photograph, a brief visit or favorite music may offer connection without asking the person to participate beyond what feels welcome.

The care-planning question is not how to reproduce a perfect occasion. It is what the person wants today, what feels tiring and what can be simplified or left out.

At Eternal Life Hospice, comfort care starts with listening to those preferences. Privacy, energy and the option to decline remain important, even when a family’s intentions are loving.

Our Journal article offers families and care partners a starting point for that conversation.
